sources.title: Neanderthal wooden tools from Spain found preserved in stone

items.title: Neanderthal Woodwork, Preserved as Hollow Molds in Spanish Stone
items.body: At Abric Romaní, a rock shelter in Capellades west of Barcelona, mineral-rich water coated Neanderthal wooden tools in a limestone-like crust. The wood itself rotted away, and the crust kept its negative: hollow molds that faithfully reflect the shape of the tools that made them. What those molds record is more than a hunting kit. The finds include spears, digging sticks, bark trays, parts of shelters, and a club unlike anything seen before — a working life in wood that the stone record alone would never have shown.

items.title: Why the Moon's Farside Has No Smooth Dark Maria
items.body: The Moon's two faces don't match. The nearside is covered in smooth dark maria, the plains that give the Moon its familiar markings; the farside is rough and battered instead. A likely explanation is thickness: if the farside crust is thicker, molten material from the interior has a harder time flowing up to the surface and pooling into those dark, smooth plains. Same body, different plumbing — and one hemisphere ends up looking like a different world.

sources.title: Residential school denialism shouldn't be illegal, Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew says

items.title: Wab Kinew Says Residential School Denialism Should Stay Legal
items.body: Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew calls residential school denialism detestable but not illegal, and argues that shouldn't change. He is pushing back on federal Manitoba New Democrat Leah Gazan's effort to add it to the Criminal Code. That leaves two elected figures from the same political tradition on opposite sides of a question with no tidy answer: whether the criminal law is the right instrument against denial of historical atrocity, or whether a state should stay out of the business of prosecuting it.

sources.title: ‘14th’ Review: Ava DuVernay’s Powerful Sequel to ‘13th’ Turns a Constitutional Amendment into Living History

discussion.body: The trap in a film about a constitutional amendment is reverence. The review's praise is that this one refuses the classroom: it treats the document as something contested rather than settled, which is a harder and more interesting register to hold for two hours.

Refusing reverence isn't the same as being neutral. Calling the Constitution a living, breathing document is an argument with consequences, not a description — the film may be taking a side while sounding like it is simply explaining.

Perhaps, but the alternative is pretending the text is finished and settled, which is the complacency the review is describing. A film that makes the Constitution feel like something we are still arguing over is at least honest about what a constitution is for.

items.title: Ava DuVernay's '14th' Wants to Make the Constitution Feel Alive
items.body: Variety's review of '14th' says the film exerts the same kind of historical and topical force as '13th', and the specific claim is about tone as much as argument. The review's point is that the film cuts through the dusty complacency with which the Constitution tends to be regarded — the way merely hearing the word can make you feel like you're back in school — and presents it instead as a living, breathing document that we fail to heed at our peril. The interesting part isn't the subject; it's the claim that a mainstream, accessible register and real historical nuance are not a trade-off here.

sources.title: What's been driving Hawaii's lava fountains?

discussion.body: Several hundred metres of molten rock is the spectacle. The more interesting problem is that nobody can yet say what drives it — the show has outrun the explanation.
Three fountaining episodes at Kilauea since 1823 is a thin record to reason from. Catching the next episode well may matter more than adding another theory.

items.title: Lava Fountains Shoot Hundreds of Metres Up. What Powers Them Isn't Settled.
items.body: At Mount Etna, in Hawaii and in Iceland, lava does not always leave the ground at a walkable pace. It gets thrown up in fountains that can reach several hundred metres in height — and what powers those fountains is still an open question. Hotspot volcanism, the setting behind several of these sites, is usually far less theatrical than that. The jets are the exception worth explaining, and the explanation isn't settled yet.

items.title: The Galaxies Bunched to One Side of a Cluster Image Aren't in the Cluster
items.body: As NASA describes it, some of the galaxies bunched together on one side of a cluster image are not part of the cluster at all. They sit much farther away, and their light has been bent and magnified by gravitational lensing — which makes apparent neighbours in a photograph into strangers separated by enormous distance along the line of sight. The lens is mass, not glass. Gravitational lensing happens when the enormous mass of a foreground object, such as a galaxy cluster, bends and magnifies light arriving from something much farther behind it. The cluster in front works like a crude magnifying glass, so the background galaxy we see is a bent and enlarged version of the original.

sources.title: Alberta Court of Appeal says Ottawa's Impact Assessment Act is still unconstitutional

items.title: Alberta's Court of Appeal Says Ottawa's Rewritten Impact Assessment Act Is Still Unconstitutional
items.body: In a decision issued Friday, Alberta's Court of Appeal held that the federal Impact Assessment Act still infringes on provincial jurisdiction — even though Ottawa amended the law after the Supreme Court struck down much of it in 2023. The amendment was supposed to be the repair job. The provincial court's answer is that the constitutional problem outlasted it, which turns a drafting exercise into an argument about where the federal boundary sits.

sources.title: Danny Trejo Insists He’s “Pro-Immigrant” & “Proud Mexican” Amid Backlash To Daily Wire’s ICE Film: “Make No Mistake”

discussion.body: Casting isn't endorsement. Actors take work, and a character's politics aren't automatically the actor's own.
Fine in the abstract, but Pawn Shop arrived with protests already attached to it. Saying yes to a production that has become a political marker is itself a choice, and it will be read as one.
Which leaves the genuinely hard question: not what Trejo believes, but whether a performance can be pulled apart from the production that surrounds it.

items.title: Danny Trejo Says He's 'Pro-Immigrant' Amid Backlash Over His Role in Pawn Shop
items.body: Danny Trejo has broken his silence over the backlash to his role in Pawn Shop, the Daily Wire production that Deadline describes as a pro-ICE film, made by Ben Shapiro's production company and Dallas Sonnier's Bonfire Legend. On Friday the LA-born Mexican-American actor insisted he is 'pro-immigrant.' The project has drawn protests from locals in Livingston, Montana. An actor's own politics and a film's politics are two different things, and Trejo is entitled to insist on the distinction. But a part in a film that has already become a political marker is not read by audiences as a neutral decision, and that is the squeeze he is in.

sources.title: How drones are hunting fires hidden beneath the Cairngorms

items.title: Why a Wildfire Can Keep Burning After the Flames Are Gone
items.body: The dramatic flames from July's huge Cairngorms wildfire are gone, but hot spots can keep burning beneath the earth. That is the odd problem drones are being used to hunt: a fire that has left the visible surface but hasn't stopped smoldering underground. The appeal of an airborne search is obvious — a hotspot under the soil isn't something you spot from a footpath, and it can persist after the blaze looks finished. What the surface shows and what the ground is doing are two different things.

sources.title: US imposes sanctions aiming to 'dismantle' International Criminal Court

discussion.body: Deutsche Welle characterizes this as the latest in a series of steps rather than an isolated action, which matters for reading the announcement as part of a pattern.
Sanctioning a court the US isn't a member of is a strange lever, but the report is explicit about the stated goal: dismantling the institution, not reforming it.

items.title: US Sanctions Target the International Criminal Court
items.body: The US has announced new sanctions on the International Criminal Court, according to Deutsche Welle. The report frames it as the latest in a series of steps by the Trump administration as it seeks to dismantle the intergovernmental organization. That is the stated aim as the outlet describes it — a campaign, not a one-off measure.

sources.title: Prize-winning image which sparked backlash was AI-generated, Nikon rules

items.title: Nikon Rules a Prize-Winning Image Was AI-Generated
items.body: The camera-maker says it is now re-evaluating the rules and procedures of its Small World in Motion contest after ruling that a prize-winning image which sparked backlash was AI-generated. The interesting wrinkle is where the judgment landed: not on the image alone, but on the contest's own machinery. A competition that judges and rewards images now has to decide what counts as one.

sources.title: ‘Exorcism of God’ Director Alejandro Hidalgo to Helm Malaysian Hungry Ghost Festival Horror ‘The Hungry One’ (EXCLUSIVE)

items.title: The 100-Year-Old Godfather Problem, This Time in Malaysia
items.body: Alejandro Hidalgo, director of “The Exorcism of God,” is set to make “The Hungry One,” a supernatural horror film unfolding over Malaysia's Hungry Ghost Festival. Kuala Lumpur-based Abnormal Studios is handling worldwide sales and introducing the project at the Busan International Film Festival's Asian Contents & Film Market, and Singapore-based Clover Films has already picked it up. The festival is a setting where a film can be sold before it exists — a market built on pitches and territory rights rather than finished reels.

items.title: What Film Noir Looked Like Before It Had a Name
items.body: Film noir is usually described as a mood before it is described as a genre, and the visual vocabulary is part of why. A dark domestic interior suffused with an insidious pall; a world aghast at the horrors of an existentialism fashioned by disenchantment and pessimism. That is the recognisable iconography of noir, in which the moral ambivalence and psychic dislocations of postwar modernity congeal upon the cinematic image. Senses of Cinema frames Marcel Carné's Thérèse Raquin (1953) inside exactly that tradition — which is the interesting wrinkle, because Carné's film sits in a French lineage that predates the American label Hollywood critics later applied. The gloom isn't decoration. It is the argument: a postwar world where the interior matches the psyche, and the shadows are doing the moral work the plot won't.

sources.title: Ke Huy Quan reflects on his family's escape from post-war Vietnam on 'Settle In'

items.title: Ke Huy Quan's Memoir Begins With the Escape, Not the Comeback
items.body: Ke Huy Quan arrived in America as a refugee, and the films that made him a recognizable face as a kid — Indiana Jones and The Goonies — came early. Then came decades away from the spotlight, and later an Oscar-winning comeback. His new memoir, Never Say Die, doesn't start with the comeback. PBS's Amna Nawaz spoke with him on the News podcast Settle In about the book, which opens with his family's harrowing attempts to escape post-war Vietnam. It's a reminder that the tidy arc usually told about Quan — child star, disappearance, redemption — is a later chapter. The book puts the family's flight first, which is presumably the point of writing it at all.

sources.title: Asana cuts model costs 76x in browser tests with GPT-6.1 Sol

items.title: Optimist: Asana Cut Its Browser Agent's Cost 76x. Skeptic: Read the Adverb.
items.body: Optimist: Asana used GPT-6 Astra in Codex to make its browser agent 76 times cheaper and 5 times faster, which is the kind of number that makes a product's unit economics stop being a problem. Skeptic: In tests. Optimist: Yes, in tests, and 76x is a big enough margin that even a badly degraded real-world result leaves room. Skeptic: That's the argument every vendor benchmark makes right before customers find out which half of the workload the tests skipped. Optimist: Fine — but a browser agent that costs 1/76th as much changes what you're willing to let it attempt, and that's a product decision, not a benchmark one. Skeptic: Agreed on that. Cheaper mistakes are still the interesting part.

sources.title: Alberta Court of Appeal says Impact Assessment Act is still unconstitutional

items.title: Alberta's Top Court Says Ottawa's Rewritten Impact Assessment Act Is Still Unconstitutional
items.body: Alberta's Court of Appeal has found that the federal Impact Assessment Act, in its revised form, remains unconstitutional. The court's reasoning centers on reach: the act, it found, still grants Ottawa the power to halt a project inside provincial jurisdiction if that project has even the smallest impact on federal jurisdiction — a threshold the court treats as too broad a hook for federal authority over projects that are otherwise provincial business. The decision keeps alive one of the sharper federalism fights over who gets to say yes or no to major energy and infrastructure projects.

sources.title: 'It was a definite quid pro quo.' GOP donor who accused Guilfoyle of corruption speaks out

items.title: A GOP Donor Says the U.S. Ambassador to Greece Asked Him for $100,000 for Access
items.body: A Republican donor is accusing Kimberly Guilfoyle, the U.S. ambassador to Greece, of asking him for $100,000 in exchange for access to top Trump administration officials — access, he argues, that was never delivered. Eric Deters, a former Kentucky congressional candidate, made the accusation and discussed the requests for payment and the promised access in an interview with PBS NewsHour's Amna Nawaz. The claim is an allegation by a named donor, not an established finding; the account is his.

sources.title: ‘14th’ Review: Ava DuVernay’s Impassioned Defense Of Constitution Takes Aim At Trump & Attempted Rescission Of Rights

items.title: Ava DuVernay's New Documentary Opens on Presidents Swearing an Oath
items.body: Ava DuVernay's documentary 14th closes the New York Film Festival, and it opens with a montage of American presidents taking the oath of office — FDR, Eisenhower, JFK, LBJ, Nixon, Carter, Reagan — each swearing to preserve, protect and defend the Constitution of the United States. Building the film's argument out of the words of the office itself is a pointed choice for a documentary Deadline frames as an impassioned defense of the Constitution aimed at Trump and what the headline calls an attempted rescission of rights. The opening does the rhetorical work before any argument arrives.

sources.title: Macron and Steinmeier struggle to revive Franco-German ties

items.title: Macron and Steinmeier Are Leaving Office as the Franco-German Engine Sputters
items.body: Both presidents are on their way out — Frank-Walter Steinmeier and Emmanuel Macron are about to step down from their offices — and a meeting between them in France made the state of the partnership plain. DW reports the encounter showed how urgently the Franco-German relationship needs new momentum. Two departing presidents trying to restart a pairing whose whole value is continuity is an awkward position to hand to whoever comes next.
